Lesson

Building the Postwar Order

Mr. MagisterYour teacher
Today's Focus

How did the wartime allies build a new world order, and why did it split in two?

When Germany surrendered in May 1945, winning the war had only started the work. This lesson follows the founding of the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions, the meetings at Yalta and Potsdam, the Soviet grip on Eastern Europe, the Iron Curtain, and the question of why Stalin acted as he did.

Objectives
  1. I will be able to explain how the United States tried to build lasting international institutions after 1945
  2. I will be able to describe how disagreement over Eastern Europe split the wartime allies
  3. I will be able to evaluate competing explanations for Soviet behavior after the war

Verdict

Why Did the Allies Split?

My Verdict

1.The lesson says the wartime allies were no longer allies by 1947, and that historians offer several explanations for Stalin's choices. Decide which explanation, or which mix of explanations, you find strongest, then defend your verdict with one fact from the book that supports your view and one fact that cuts against it.

The chapters give three views of Stalin: safety, belief, and a system that needed enemies. They also say careful historians do not choose just one, and that his character shaped his choices. Facts to weigh include what he promised at Yalta, what happened in Poland, Romania, and Czechoslovakia, and the fact that Russia had been invaded twice in thirty years.

My Notebook
Keep This in Mind

The wartime allies built the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions, but disagreement over Eastern Europe split them. By 1947 journalists were calling the struggle a cold war.

The Postwar Order and Containment

Building the Postwar Order

Part 1

A New World Order

Chapter 1A Lesson from 1919 and the Security Council
Chapter 2Bretton Woods
Chapter 1

A Lesson from 1919 and the Security Council

When Germany surrendered in May 1945, the leaders of the great powers knew that winning the war had only started their work. Europe and much of Asia lay in ruins. Britain and France were worn out and deep in debt. In Germany, cities were piles of rubble, and millions of refugees and former prisoners were on the road, looking for homes that no longer existed. Britain, which had gone without bread rationing during the war, began rationing bread in 1946. Only two countries came out of the war stronger. One was the United States, whose factories had grown to produce about half of the world's manufactured goods. The other was the Soviet Union, which had lost more than twenty million people but now held the largest army in Europe. The question was whether these two powers would build a lasting peace together, or divide the world between them.

The United States had been through this once before. In 1919, Woodrow Wilson had asked the country to join a League of Nations, and the Senate had said no. A treaty needs two thirds of the Senate to pass, and Wilson, who had refused to bargain with the senators who objected, fell short. Franklin Roosevelt had watched that happen, and he was determined not to repeat it. He planned a new organization early, and he brought leading senators into the planning. Members of both parties went to San Francisco as part of the American delegation, so that the Senate would feel the charter was partly its own. In the spring of 1945, delegates from fifty nations met in San Francisco to write the charter of the United Nations. The work took two months. The charter was signed on June 26, 1945, and the delegates went home to win approval from their own governments. The smaller nations disliked the idea that five great powers could block any action, but the great powers made it clear that there would be no organization without that right. This time the Senate approved it in July 1945, by a vote of 89 to 2. The United Nations came into existence that fall, and its headquarters were later built in New York City.

The new body had a design that showed how Roosevelt thought. Every member state had a seat in a General Assembly. But the real power sat in a smaller body, the Security Council, which could order action to keep the peace. Five nations held permanent seats there: the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France, and China. Each one held a veto, which is the power to block a decision by voting no, even if every other member votes yes. The General Assembly, where each nation had one vote, could debate and recommend, but only the Security Council could order action. Roosevelt believed that no peace could last unless the great powers agreed to it. He also knew that the veto might paralyze the council when those powers disagreed. In the first ten years alone, the Soviet Union used the veto dozens of times, and its diplomat Andrei Gromyko earned the nickname "Mr. No." That is exactly what happened in the years that followed.

Chapter 2

Bretton Woods

The United States also tried to fix the economic problems that had helped cause the war. In July 1944, delegates from forty-four nations met at a resort in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire. The meeting took place in a large hotel in the White Mountains, less than two months after the invasion of Normandy. The Bretton Woods Conference set up two institutions. The International Monetary Fund was meant to steady the value of national currencies and lend money to countries in short-term trouble. Here is how that was supposed to work. If a country ran short of dollars to pay for imports, it could borrow from the fund instead of putting a tariff on foreign goods or letting its money collapse in value. The World Bank was meant to lend money for rebuilding and development. The delegates also agreed that other currencies would be tied to the dollar, and the dollar would be tied to gold at thirty-five dollars an ounce. The British economist John Maynard Keynes and the American official Harry Dexter White did much of the planning, and they did not always agree. The Soviet Union sent delegates but never joined. The plan worked only because the United States held most of the world's gold, so the dollar was the one currency everyone trusted. The new institutions did not begin lending until 1947. The goal was to avoid a repeat of the 1930s, when tariff wars and money troubles had choked trade. In the language of this course, it was an attempt to solve a first-order economic problem: how to make sure nations could trade and prosper.

Part 2

The Alliance Breaks

Chapter 3Yalta, Truman, and the Iron Curtain
Chapter 3

Yalta, Truman, and the Iron Curtain

Meanwhile, the Big Three had met to decide the shape of the peace. In February 1945, Roosevelt, Churchill, and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin gathered at the Yalta Conference in the Crimea, in a former palace of the Russian tsars. By then the Red Army had already pushed into Poland and stood within about fifty miles of Berlin. They agreed to divide a defeated Germany into zones of occupation. Stalin promised to enter the war against Japan after Germany fell. He also promised "free and unfettered elections" in Poland. The Soviets had already set up a Polish government made up of communists. At Yalta, Stalin agreed that other Poles would be added to it and that free elections would follow. The Big Three also settled how the veto would work and agreed that two Soviet republics, Ukraine and Belarus, would get seats in the General Assembly. Roosevelt, who was ill and tired, left Yalta hopeful. Two months later he was dead.

His successor, Harry Truman, had been vice president for only eighty-two days. Roosevelt had told him almost nothing about the war's biggest secrets, including the atomic bomb. Truman had to learn quickly. Eleven days after taking office, he met the Soviet foreign minister, Vyacheslav Molotov, at the White House and told him bluntly that the Soviets must keep their promises about Poland. Truman later recalled that Molotov said he had never been talked to that way. At the Potsdam meeting in July 1945, he sat across the table from Stalin and found that the Yalta promises about Poland meant very little to the Soviet leader. The leaders also accepted a new western border for Poland, which meant that millions of Germans were forced out of the lands Poland gained.

The Red Army had driven the Germans out of Eastern Europe, and it did not leave. In Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Hungary, and, after a coup in 1948, Czechoslovakia, local communists backed by Soviet power took control. Elections were rigged or put off. In Hungary, communists removed their rivals one slice at a time, a method that their leader himself called "salami tactics." In Romania, a Soviet official walked into the king's palace in 1945 and demanded a government led by communists. In Poland, the election of January 1947 was so rigged that the Western powers protested, and the leader of the main opposition party, Stanislaw Mikolajczyk, fled the country soon afterward. Czechoslovakia was a harder case, because it had held a free election in 1946, and communists had won about a third of the vote. In February 1948, they took over the government with Soviet backing, and weeks later the foreign minister, Jan Masaryk, who was not a communist, was found dead below a window. These countries became satellite states, which are nations that keep the outward form of independence but are controlled by a stronger neighbor. In March 1946, Winston Churchill spoke at a small college in Fulton, Missouri, with Truman, who had traveled with him by train, sitting on the platform. Churchill held no office at the time, having lost the British election the summer before. "From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic," he said, "an iron curtain has descended across the Continent." The phrase Iron Curtain stuck. Stalin answered in the newspaper Pravda, comparing Churchill to Hitler and calling him a warmonger.

Part 3

Why, and What Came Next

Chapter 4Why Did Stalin Do It, and Bringing the Troops Home
Chapter 5Occupation, Nuremberg, and the Cold War
Chapter 4

Why Did Stalin Do It, and Bringing the Troops Home

Why did Stalin do this? Historians still argue about it, and the answer matters. One view says that Stalin was mainly worried about safety. Russia had been invaded twice by Germany in thirty years, and he wanted a belt of friendly states to protect him. A second view says that he was moved by his beliefs. A communist state, in this view, could not feel secure until its neighbors were communist too. A third says that the Soviet system, which ran on fear and a constant search for enemies, needed foreign threats to justify itself. The most careful historians do not choose just one. They point out that Stalin was a suspicious and ruthless man, and that his character, not just his country's geography, shaped the choices he made. A different Soviet leader might have acted differently.

The Americans did not leave Europe, as they had in 1919, but they did something that Americans had always done after a war: they sent the soldiers home. Families demanded it, and thousands of troops held protests overseas. The army sent soldiers home by a point system based on months of service, time overseas, and medals earned, and soldiers who still waited felt it moved too slowly. In January 1946, GIs held demonstrations in Manila, Paris, and other cities, and Congress was flooded with letters from their families. Between 1945 and 1947, the armed forces shrank from about twelve million men and women to fewer than two million. A republic does not like to keep a large army in peacetime, and the founders had warned against it. The Soviet Union also sent soldiers home, but it kept several million under arms. The cost was that, in 1946, the United States had far less force in Europe than the Soviet army.

Chapter 5

Occupation, Nuremberg, and the Cold War

Even so, some troops stayed. American forces occupied western Germany, and General Douglas MacArthur ruled Japan, where he oversaw a new constitution that was written in 1946 and took effect in 1947. Occupation officials also bought land from large landowners and sold it cheaply to the farmers who worked it, so that many tenant farmers became owners. MacArthur's staff wrote the first draft in about a week. The emperor stayed on the throne, but only as a symbol, and he told his people that he was not a god. It gave the Japanese a parliament and the vote for women. In one article, Japan renounced war. That article also said that Japan would not keep an army, navy, or air force. The occupation of Japan is often seen as one of the most successful rebuilding projects in American history.

The Allies also decided that the leaders of Nazi Germany should answer for their crimes in a court, not be shot without a trial. In November 1945, judges from the United States, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union began hearing the case at Nuremberg, a city where the Nazis had once held huge rallies. The charges included waging aggressive war and what the prosecutors called crimes against humanity, a phrase that had hardly been used in a court before. The trial lasted nearly a year. Twelve of the defendants were sentenced to death, and three were set free. A similar court in Tokyo tried Japanese leaders, including former Prime Minister Tojo, who was hanged in 1948.

By 1947, the wartime allies were no longer allies. Each side blamed the other. They did not fight a direct war, since each had the power to destroy the other, but they struggled for influence over every part of the world. Journalists began to call this struggle the Cold War, because it was fought with spies, money, alliances, propaganda, and threats instead of direct combat. The financier Bernard Baruch used the term in a speech in April 1947, and the columnist Walter Lippmann soon made it famous. The next lesson explains how the United States answered the Soviet challenge, and why the strategy it chose became known by a single word.
